Part 1 of 12

Why the Rules Matter: The Road to the Nomination

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 1: Essential Question: How do the structural mechanics of American elections shape the strategic behavior of candidates and the ultimate expression of popular sovereignty?

FQ 2: Differentiate between the primary and general election phases of a political campaign, explaining how the distinct audiences, rules, and incentive structures of each phase shape candidate strategy, messaging, and resource allocation.

IN MY WORDS: Think about a game you know well. How could changing one rule change the way people play?

Reading AThe Election That Broke the Rules

On the evening of November 4, 1800, the outcome of the presidential election was not yet known, and it would not be resolved for months. The contest between John Adams and Thomas Jefferson — the second time these two foundational figures of the republic had faced each other for the nation's highest office — produced not just a change of power but a constitutional crisis. Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr received the same number of electoral votes, throwing the election into the House of Representatives, where thirty-six ballots were required before Jefferson was finally declared the winner. The election of 1800 was, by any measure, the most dramatic and consequential electoral contest in American history — and it revealed, in the republic's first decade of existence, that the mechanisms through which Americans chose their leaders were as consequential as the leaders themselves.

Word help: electoral votes = the votes that decide who becomes president · House of Representatives = the part of Congress with members based on state population · constitutional crisis = a serious problem about what the Constitution allows · consequential = very important · mechanisms = the ways something works

Chapter 14, Introduction.

Reading BWhy the Rules Are Never Neutral

But elections are not simply moments of popular expression; they are highly structured, legally regulated, and strategically contested competitions in which the rules of the game shape the strategies of the competitors in profound and sometimes counterintuitive ways. The structure of the primary system, the logic of the Electoral College, the legal framework governing campaign finance, and the demographic patterns of voter participation all determine not just who wins elections but what kinds of candidates run, what policies they advocate, and whose preferences the political system ultimately serves.

Understanding elections means understanding these historical layers — and understanding that the rules that govern who wins power are never neutral, never permanent, and always contested.

Word help: popular expression = people showing what they want · legally regulated = controlled by laws · strategically contested = fought over with careful plans · advocate = to speak in favor of · historical layers = rules added in different time periods · neutral = not favoring either side

Chapter 14, Introduction.

Reading CFour Parts of a Campaign

Understanding American elections requires understanding the full arc of the campaign process: the grueling internal competition of the nomination phase, during which candidates must win their own party's support before they can face the opposition; the general election phase, in which the strategic calculus shifts from appealing to partisan base voters to assembling the coalition needed to win a majority of Electoral College votes; the permanent and escalating battle over campaign finance, in which the constitutional protection of political speech continuously collides with democratic concerns about the disproportionate influence of organized money; and the patterns of voter participation that determine which segments of the American public actually exercise their formal right to choose their government.

Word help: arc = the whole path from start to finish · nomination = being chosen as a party's candidate · general election = the final election between the parties' candidates · coalition = a group of different voters who join together · campaign finance = how campaigns raise and spend money · voter participation = how many people actually vote · formal right = a right written in law

Reading DFrom Smoke-Filled Rooms to Popular Primaries

The direct primary — the election in which registered voters, rather than party officials, choose the party's nominee — emerged in the early twentieth century as a product of the Progressive movement's sustained campaign against what reformers viewed as the corrupt, undemocratic power of party machines. In cities like New York, Chicago, and Philadelphia, the dominant party organizations of the late nineteenth century had perfected the art of controlling nominations: picking candidates who were loyal to the machine, rewarding supporters with government jobs and contracts, and delivering votes through a combination of patronage, community organization, and when necessary, outright fraud. The direct primary was designed to cut through this web of organizational control and restore the nomination decision to the party's rank-and-file supporters.

The adoption of primaries for presidential nominations was more gradual and more contested than their use in state and local races. For much of the twentieth century, presidential nominations remained substantially under the control of party leaders who gathered at national conventions with significant discretion to negotiate and bargain over the eventual nominee. The turning point came after the chaotic 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, where Vice President Hubert Humphrey secured the nomination without having won a single primary election, amid bitter intra-party conflict over the Vietnam War and violent clashes between police and anti-war demonstrators outside the convention hall. The sense that the nomination process had been captured by party insiders at the expense of the party's actual voters produced a sweeping reform effort — led by the McGovern-Fraser Commission — that fundamentally restructured the Democratic primary process to give rank-and-file voters a decisive role in delegate selection. Republicans made parallel, if less dramatic, reforms in subsequent years.

Word help: direct primary = an election where voters, not party leaders, pick the party's candidate · Progressive movement = early 1900s reformers who fought corruption · party machines = strong party groups that controlled jobs and votes · patronage = giving government jobs as rewards · rank-and-file = ordinary members · brokered convention = a convention where leaders make deals to pick a nominee · intra-party = inside one party · McGovern-Fraser Commission = the Democratic reform group of 1968-72

Part 2 of 12

Primaries, Caucuses, and Momentum

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 2: Differentiate between the primary and general election phases of a political campaign, explaining how the distinct audiences, rules, and incentive structures of each phase shape candidate strategy, messaging, and resource allocation.

IN MY WORDS: If you could vote in only one party's primary, would you want to? Why or why not?

Reading EClosed and Open Primaries

A closed primary is one in which participation is restricted to voters who have registered with the party in advance — typically weeks or months before the election itself. Only registered Democrats may vote in a closed Democratic primary; only registered Republicans may vote in a closed Republican primary. The logic of the closed primary reflects a particular theory of what primary elections are for: they are the internal decision-making process of a private political organization, and the right to participate in that process should be reserved for individuals who have made a meaningful commitment to the party by registering as members. Closed primaries tend to produce electorates that are more ideologically homogeneous than the general electorate — since the voters who register with a party and participate in its primary tend to hold more consistently partisan views than the broader public — which generally advantages candidates who appeal to the party's ideological base rather than its moderate center.

An open primary takes the opposite approach: any registered voter may participate in either party's primary regardless of their own party registration, or in some variants, voters may participate without any prior registration at all. Some states allow registered independents to choose which party's primary to vote in on Election Day; others allow any voter to participate in any primary. The open primary reflects a different theory: that primary elections are a public function, conducted with public resources and serving the public interest in producing qualified candidates, and that participation should therefore be broadly available. Open primaries tend to produce more moderate nominees because the electorate includes not just committed partisans but independents and occasionally cross-party voters who may prefer candidates closer to the political center.

Word help: closed primary = only registered party members may vote · open primary = voters may choose either party's primary · homogeneous = all alike · partisan = strongly loyal to one party · advantages = helps · independents = voters who belong to no party · public function = a job done for everyone, with public money

Reading FA Choice With Consequences

The choice between open and closed primaries is not merely a technical administrative question; it is a consequential political decision about the character of the nomination process and the candidates it produces. In a closed primary system, party activists and ideologically committed voters exercise disproportionate influence over who becomes the nominee, which can produce candidates whose positions are well-calibrated to the party base but may be less appealing to the general electorate. In an open primary system, the influence of independents and moderate voters can pull nominations toward the center, but it also opens the possibility of strategic voting — the deliberate participation of voters in a rival party's primary for the purpose of choosing a weaker opponent, rather than out of any genuine preference among the candidates.

Word help: administrative = about running an office or process · calibrated = adjusted carefully to fit · general electorate = all the voters in the final election · strategic voting = voting for someone you do not truly prefer to get a result you want · deliberate = done on purpose

Chapter 14, Section I, “Open and Closed Primaries.”

Both sides of the rule. Use Reading F. Name one risk of closed primaries and one risk of open primaries that the chapter describes.

Reading GThe Iowa Effect and Momentum

One of the most distinctive and most criticized features of the American presidential nomination process is the extraordinary influence wielded by a small number of states that hold their primaries or caucuses very early in the election calendar. Iowa, which by tradition holds the nation's first nominating contest — a caucus system in which voters gather in person at schools, churches, and community centers to deliberate and publicly declare their preferences — and New Hampshire, which holds the nation's first primary election, have occupied positions of outsized influence in the presidential nomination process for decades. The attention, resources, and media coverage lavished on these early contests is entirely disproportionate to their size, demographic representativeness, or electoral weight in the general election — a disproportion that has generated persistent criticism and intermittent reform efforts without fundamentally altering the early calendar's structure.

The influence of early states is rooted in the dynamics of momentum in the primary process. A candidate who performs strongly in Iowa and New Hampshire — even if they win by a narrow margin or simply exceed expectations — receives a surge of favorable media coverage that shapes perceptions of their viability for weeks afterward. Donors who had been hedging their bets between multiple candidates consolidate their support behind the perceived front-runner. Endorsers who had been holding back publicly commit. Rival campaigns, watching their fundraising dry up in the wake of disappointing early results, find themselves unable to sustain the organizational infrastructure needed to compete in the states that follow. Candidates who struggle in Iowa and New Hampshire often withdraw from the race entirely before many states have even begun their primary process, effectively leaving the final choice of nominee to the small and unrepresentative electorates of two relatively homogeneous early states.

Word help: caucus = a meeting where voters gather and publicly show their choice · deliberate = think and talk carefully · disproportionate = much bigger than it should be · demographic = about the makeup of a population · momentum = a growing sense that a candidate is winning · front-runner = the candidate who seems to be ahead · viable = able to succeed · infrastructure = the staff and offices a campaign needs

Chapter 14, Section I, “The Iowa Effect and the Strategy of Frontloading.”

Reading HFrontloading

This dynamic has produced the phenomenon political scientists call frontloading: the tendency of states to move their primaries earlier in the calendar in order to capture the strategic benefits of early-state influence — the media attention, the candidate visits, the economic activity generated by major campaigns operating at full intensity. As more states moved their primaries earlier, the effective primary season compressed, creating a situation in which candidates face a rapid-fire sequence of contests in multiple states simultaneously rather than the more deliberate state-by-state process that characterized earlier nomination contests. The compressed calendar rewards candidates who enter the race with strong name recognition, established fundraising networks, and the organizational infrastructure to compete in multiple states at once — structural advantages that tend to favor better-known, better-funded candidates over lesser-known insurgents, even when the insurgents may hold positions with broad appeal among the party's voters.

Word help: frontloading = states moving their primaries earlier · phenomenon = something that happens and can be studied · compressed = squeezed into less time · name recognition = how many people already know a candidate · insurgents = outsider candidates challenging the favorites · state-by-state = one state after another

Chapter 14, Section I, “The Iowa Effect and the Strategy of Frontloading.”

The General Election and the Electoral College

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 2: Differentiate between the primary and general election phases of a political campaign, explaining how the distinct audiences, rules, and incentive structures of each phase shape candidate strategy, messaging, and resource allocation.

FQ 3: Analyze the strategic importance of the Electoral College and its impact on how presidential campaigns allocate time, money, and attention — including the winner-take-all rule, the battleground state phenomenon, and the small-state advantage.

IN MY WORDS: Which two or three states do you think presidential candidates visit most? Why those?

Reading IFrom Primary to General

When the nomination contests conclude and the two major parties have selected their nominees, the strategic calculus of the presidential campaign undergoes a fundamental transformation. The primary phase, with its focus on mobilizing partisan base voters and navigating ideologically diverse party electorates, gives way to the general election phase, with its requirement to assemble a coalition broad enough to win a majority of Electoral College votes. The transition between these phases is one of the most consequential strategic moments in any presidential campaign — the moment when candidates who have spent months appealing to their party's most committed supporters must begin the delicate task of expanding their appeal to the independents and moderate voters who typically decide the outcome.

Word help: calculus = a way of weighing choices · transformation = a big change · ideologically diverse = holding many different political views · majority = more than half · moderate = not extreme · delicate = needing great care

Reading JHow the Electoral College Works

The Electoral College is among the most distinctive and most debated features of the American constitutional system. Created by the Framers in 1787 as a compromise between those who wanted the president selected by Congress and those who wanted direct popular election, the Electoral College was designed to filter the popular will through the judgment of informed electors chosen by each state. In practice, the filtering function the Framers intended has long since disappeared — today, presidential electors are expected to vote for the candidate who wins their state's popular vote, and the vast majority of states legally require them to do so — but the structural features of the system retain enormous strategic significance.

The mathematics of the Electoral College begin with the allocation of electors. Each state receives a number of electoral votes equal to its total congressional delegation — its House seats plus its two senators. This means that every state, regardless of population, receives a minimum of three electoral votes — two for its senators and at least one for its House member. California, the nation's most populous state, receives fifty-four electoral votes; Wyoming, the least populous, receives three. A candidate needs to win a majority of the 538 total electoral votes — at least 270 — to be elected president. If no candidate achieves this threshold, the election is decided by the House of Representatives, with each state delegation casting a single vote — the same procedure that resolved the disputed election of 1800.

Word help: Electoral College = the system where states' electors choose the president · electors = the people chosen by each state to cast its electoral votes · compromise = a deal where each side gives something up · congressional delegation = a state's House members plus its senators · plurality = the most votes, even if not a majority · threshold = the number needed to win · strategic = connected to planning to win

Chapter 14, Section II, “The Architecture of the Electoral College.”

Source AHamilton on Electors

Alexander Hamilton wrote this in 1788 to persuade New York to ratify the Constitution. He explained why the Framers chose electors.

“It was desirable, that the sense of the people should operate in the choice of the person to whom so important a trust was to be confided.”
“A small number of persons, selected by their fellow-citizens from the general mass, will be most likely to possess the information and discernment requisite to such complicated investigations.”

Word help: desirable = something good to have · the sense of the people = what the people think · confided = trusted to someone · selected = chosen · the general mass = ordinary citizens · discernment = good judgment · requisite = needed · investigations = careful study

Reading KWinner-Take-All

The most strategically consequential feature of the Electoral College is the winner-take-all rule that governs forty-eight of the fifty states. In these states, the candidate who wins a plurality of the popular vote — even if that plurality is a single vote — receives all of the state's electoral votes. The remaining two states — Maine and Nebraska — allocate some of their electoral votes by congressional district, making it possible for the two candidates to split a state's electoral votes, though this is rare in practice. The winner-take-all rule produces campaign dynamics that are radically different from what would emerge under a national popular vote, because it makes the margin of victory within any state irrelevant to the Electoral College outcome. Running up a large margin of victory in a state that you would have won anyway produces no additional electoral votes; the strategic premium is on winning states, not on winning them by large margins.

Word help: winner-take-all = the winner of a state gets all of its electoral votes · plurality = the most votes · by congressional district = separately in each U.S. House district · national popular vote = counting every vote in the country together · irrelevant = not mattering · margin = the size of a lead

Battleground States, the Electoral College Debate, and Incumbency

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 2: Differentiate between the primary and general election phases of a political campaign, explaining how the distinct audiences, rules, and incentive structures of each phase shape candidate strategy, messaging, and resource allocation.

FQ 3: Analyze the strategic importance of the Electoral College and its impact on how presidential campaigns allocate time, money, and attention — including the winner-take-all rule, the battleground state phenomenon, and the small-state advantage.

IN MY WORDS: Does your vote feel powerful or small? What makes you feel that way?

Reading LBattleground States

The winner-take-all structure of the Electoral College, combined with the strong partisan leanings of most states, produces the defining strategic reality of modern presidential campaigns: the concentration of candidate attention, advertising spending, and organizational effort in a small number of genuinely competitive states while the majority of the country is effectively ignored. The logic is straightforward: a Democratic presidential candidate who campaigns intensively in California is spending resources to accumulate a larger margin of victory in a state they will win regardless. A Republican who campaigns in Texas is doing the same. Neither state's outcome is in genuine doubt; pouring resources into them produces no strategic benefit.

The consequence is that presidential campaigns focus their finite resources — time, advertising dollars, staff, and candidate visits — almost exclusively on the states where the outcome is genuinely uncertain. These battleground states or swing states — in recent cycles most prominently Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, and North Carolina — are the actual sites of the presidential election. Their voters are courted with relentless advertising, personal candidate visits, intensive ground-level organizing, and targeted appeals. The residents of reliably partisan states, by contrast, may go an entire campaign season without seeing a presidential candidate in person, without being targeted by the campaign's television advertising, and without feeling that their individual votes have any meaningful impact on the outcome.

Word help: battleground states = states where either party could win · swing states = another name for battleground states · reliably partisan = almost always votes for the same party · finite = limited · ground-level organizing = door-to-door and local work · targeted appeals = messages aimed at certain voters

Chapter 14, Section II, “Battleground States and the Geography of Presidential Campaigns.”

Reading MThe Critics' Case

This concentration of campaign activity in battleground states has generated persistent criticism that the Electoral College distorts democratic representation, creating a system in which some citizens' votes are functionally more consequential than others' based solely on the partisan composition of the state in which they happen to live. A voter in Ohio who is the margin of victory in a closely contested state exercises far more practical influence over the presidential election than a voter in New York or Texas who contributes to a predetermined outcome. The small-state advantage built into the Electoral College — which gives voters in small states mathematically more electoral weight per person than voters in large states — adds a second dimension to this representational distortion, though its practical significance is partially offset by the small states' tendency to be reliably partisan rather than genuinely competitive.

Word help: concentration = putting most things in one place · distorts = twists out of shape · representation = having your views counted · functionally = in how it really works · small-state advantage = small states get more electoral weight per person · mathematically = by the numbers · offset = balanced out

Chapter 14, Section II, “Battleground States and the Geography of Presidential Campaigns.”

Reading NThe Defenders' Case

Defenders of the Electoral College argue that its geographic logic produces important democratic benefits that a national popular vote would not. By requiring candidates to build geographically diverse coalitions rather than simply maximizing their national vote total, the Electoral College arguably encourages attention to regional and local concerns that might otherwise be submerged in a nationwide competition for votes. It produces clear, decisive outcomes in most elections — a winner with a majority of electoral votes rather than a plurality of a fragmented popular vote — and it maintains the federal character of presidential elections by keeping states as the relevant unit of competition. The periodic divergence between the popular vote winner and the Electoral College winner — which occurred in 2000 and 2016 — has renewed debate about the system's democratic legitimacy, but the constitutional barriers to reform are substantial, requiring either a constitutional amendment or a coordinated interstate compact that has made significant but incomplete progress toward the threshold needed to take effect.

Word help: geographic logic = the idea that places matter · submerged = buried or hidden · plurality = the most votes, not a majority · fragmented = split into many pieces · federal character = the idea that states are a basic part of the system · legitimacy = being seen as fair and right · constitutional amendment = a change to the Constitution · interstate compact = an agreement among states

Reading OIncumbency: Name Recognition

One of the most consistent findings of electoral research is that candidates running for reelection — incumbents — hold a substantial structural advantage over challengers in most races. This incumbency advantage operates through several distinct mechanisms, each of which reflects a genuine benefit of holding office that challengers cannot easily replicate regardless of their own qualifications or resources.

The most fundamental component of the incumbency advantage is name recognition — the simple fact that voters know who their current representative is, what party they belong to, and in most cases at least something about their record. Challengers must invest enormous resources simply to reach the threshold of public awareness that incumbents possess automatically. In House races, which typically receive limited media coverage outside of major urban markets, many challengers never succeed in establishing the public presence needed to mount a serious challenge, regardless of the merits of their campaign. The cost of building name recognition from scratch is one of the primary reasons why congressional challengers face such daunting fundraising challenges: donors who evaluate candidates on the basis of their viability are reluctant to invest in a challenger who has not yet demonstrated the public profile needed to be competitive.

Word help: incumbent = the person who already holds the office · structural advantage = an advantage built into the system · mechanisms = ways something works · name recognition = how many voters know who someone is · threshold = the minimum level · viability = a real chance to win

Chapter 14, Section II, “The Incumbency Advantage and the Logic of Reelection.”

Reading POfficial Resources and Fundraising

Beyond name recognition, incumbents benefit from the "franking privilege" — the ability to send official communications to constituents at government expense — and from the staff and resources of their official offices, which enable them to provide constituent services, respond to problems, and maintain ongoing visibility in their districts throughout their term, not just during the campaign season. These official resources cannot legally be used for overtly political purposes, but the goodwill and visibility generated by effective constituent service is a political asset that incumbents accumulate continuously between elections. Additionally, incumbents typically enter reelection campaigns with established fundraising networks, experienced campaign staff, and relationships with interest groups and donors that challengers must build from the beginning.

Word help: franking privilege = sending official mail to voters at government cost · constituents = the people an official represents · constituent services = help with problems such as lost benefits · overtly political = clearly about winning votes · goodwill = people's good feeling · asset = something valuable to have · networks = groups of connected people

Part 5 of 12

Money in Campaigns: Speech Versus Influence

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 4: Evaluate the role of money in American politics, specifically the constitutional tension between the regulation of campaign finance and the First Amendment's protection of political speech, tracing the evolution of campaign finance law from the Federal Election Campaign Act through Citizens United.

IN MY WORDS: Is spending money on a campaign a kind of speech? Write what you think before you read.

Reading QWatergate and the FEC

No feature of the modern American electoral process has generated more sustained legal controversy, more ideological conflict, or more consequential Supreme Court decisions than the regulation of campaign finance. The question at the heart of this debate is one of the most fundamental in democratic theory: should the amount of money a candidate or their supporters can spend in an election campaign be limited, or does the First Amendment's protection of political speech preclude such limits? The legal and political history of campaign finance regulation over the past half-century is the story of repeated attempts to reconcile these competing values — and of the persistent failure to achieve a stable resolution.

The modern framework of federal campaign finance regulation emerged directly from the Watergate scandal of the early 1970s. Among the many abuses of the Nixon reelection campaign that the Watergate investigation exposed was a systematic pattern of illegal campaign contributions — large cash donations from corporations and wealthy individuals that were concealed from public disclosure and used to fund illegal activities, including the Watergate break-in itself. The scandal created the political momentum for comprehensive campaign finance reform, which Congress enacted in the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1974 — a landmark law that created the Federal Election Commission as an independent enforcement agency, established limits on contributions to political candidates, required public disclosure of campaign contributions and expenditures, and created a system of public financing for presidential campaigns.

Word help: campaign finance = money raised and spent to win elections · preclude = make impossible · reconcile = bring two things into agreement · Watergate = the 1970s scandal that ended the Nixon presidency · Federal Election Campaign Act = the 1974 law on campaign money · Federal Election Commission = the agency that enforces the law · disclosure = telling the public who gave money · public financing = government money for campaigns

Chapter 14, Section III, “Campaign Finance: The Cost of Admission.”

Visual EThe Watergate Complex

This photograph appears in the chapter. The Watergate scandal led Congress to pass new campaign finance rules.

What to look for: The scandal is named for this building complex in Washington. Think about why secret cash gifts led Congress to demand disclosure.

The Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. Image from the chapter (Chapter 14, Figure 5).

Reading RBuckley v. Valeo

The new law was immediately challenged in court by a coalition of political actors across the ideological spectrum who argued that limits on campaign spending violated the First Amendment's protection of political speech. In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the Supreme Court handed down a decision that shaped the entire subsequent development of campaign finance law. The Court accepted the government's argument that large contributions to candidates created a constitutionally sufficient risk of corruption — or at least the appearance of corruption — to justify contribution limits. But it rejected the parallel argument for spending limits. A candidate's decision to spend their own money on their own campaign, the Court held, is a direct expression of political speech that the government cannot restrict without the kind of compelling justification that the risk of corruption of a self-funded candidate does not provide. More broadly, the Court established the principle that spending money to communicate political messages is itself a constitutionally protected form of expression — a principle that has defined and constrained every subsequent attempt at campaign finance reform.

Word help: challenged = taken to court · First Amendment = the part of the Constitution protecting speech, press, and other freedoms · ideological spectrum = the range from liberal to conservative · quid pro quo = something given in return for something else · corruption = using public power for private gain · compelling justification = a very strong reason · expression = a way of showing your ideas

Chapter 14, Section III, “From Watergate to the FEC.”

Source BThe Court on Money and Speech

In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the Supreme Court explained why limits on spending can reduce political speech.

“A restriction on the amount of money a person or group can spend on political communication during a campaign necessarily reduces the quantity of expression by restricting the number of issues discussed, the depth of their exploration, and the size of the audience reached. This is because virtually every means of communicating ideas in today's mass society requires the expenditure of money.”

Word help: restriction = a limit · communication = sharing ideas · necessarily = it must happen · quantity = amount · exploration = looking deeply into something · audience = the people who hear or see it · virtually = almost · expenditure = spending

Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 (1976), per curiam opinion. Cornell Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/424/1). Primary source.

The Court's logic. In your own words, why did the Court say that limiting spending limits speech? Then explain how this fits the Court's rule about contributions and expenditures in Reading R.

Reading SThe Soft Money Loophole

The Buckley framework drew a line that has proven increasingly difficult to maintain: contributions could be limited because they create a risk of quid pro quo corruption, but expenditures could not be limited because they represent independent expression. This distinction produced a series of regulatory problems as campaigns and their supporters developed sophisticated techniques for moving political money from the regulated contribution category to the unregulated expenditure category. The rise of soft money — large, unlimited contributions to political parties ostensibly designated for "party-building" activities rather than candidate advocacy — became one of the most significant of these techniques, allowing corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals to channel money into campaigns in ways that effectively evaded the contribution limits the law established.

Word help: framework = a basic structure of rules · expenditures = money spent · independent expression = speech not controlled by a candidate · soft money = large, unlimited gifts to parties for 'party-building' · ostensibly = said to be, on the surface · advocacy = speaking in favor of something · evaded = avoided

Chapter 14, Section III, “From Watergate to the FEC.”

Reading TMcCain-Feingold and Citizens United

The accumulation of soft money in the late 1980s and 1990s — which grew from a marginal practice to a multi-hundred-million-dollar industry that effectively overwhelmed the contribution limits the 1974 law had established — eventually produced a new round of reform. The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, known as the McCain-Feingold Act after its Senate sponsors, attempted to close the soft money loophole by prohibiting national party committees from raising or spending soft money, requiring that all national party fundraising be conducted under the "hard money" limits of the existing contribution cap system. The Act also imposed new restrictions on "electioneering communications" — broadcast advertisements that mentioned a federal candidate by name within thirty days of a primary or sixty days of a general election — regardless of whether those advertisements explicitly advocated for or against the candidate.

McCain-Feingold represented the most ambitious attempt at campaign finance reform since 1974, and it temporarily succeeded in redirecting some of the money flows that had accumulated outside the regulated system. But it was almost immediately challenged in court, and the restrictions it placed on electioneering communications proved constitutionally fragile. The decisive blow came with Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), discussed in Chapter 13, which struck down the prohibition on corporate-funded electioneering communications and established that the First Amendment prevents the government from restricting independent political expenditures by corporations, associations, and unions. The practical consequence — the rapid development of the Super PAC — transformed the campaign finance landscape in ways that have not been reversed.

Word help: Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act = the 2002 law known as McCain-Feingold · hard money = money under the legal contribution limits · electioneering communications = ads that name a candidate close to an election · constitutionally fragile = likely to be struck down · decisive blow = the act that ended it · Super PAC = a group that can raise and spend unlimited money independently · landscape = the whole situation

Chapter 14, Section III, “McCain-Feingold, Citizens United, and the Transformation of Modern Campaign Finance.”

Visual FCampaign Finance Law: Four Turning Points

This timeline was built for this assignment from the chapter's description of the laws and cases.

Timeline built for this assignment from Chapter 14, Section III (illustration).

Reading USuper PACs and 527 Groups

In the Super PAC era, major presidential and congressional campaigns operate in a complex ecosystem in which official campaigns — subject to contribution limits and disclosure requirements — exist alongside "shadow campaigns" consisting of Super PACs that can raise and spend unlimited funds on advertising, voter contact, and opposition research, subject only to the requirement of legal non-coordination with the official campaign. The 527 groups — named for the section of the Internal Revenue Code that governs them — represent another category of outside political organization that can engage in voter mobilization, issue advocacy, and other political activities without being subject to the contribution limits that govern official campaigns, as long as their primary purpose is not the direct election or defeat of a specific candidate. The cumulative effect of these outside organizations is to dramatically increase the total amount of money flowing through the political system while simultaneously reducing the transparency and accountability that contribution limits and disclosure requirements are supposed to provide.

Word help: ecosystem = a system where many parts depend on each other · shadow campaigns = outside groups working alongside a campaign · non-coordination = not working together with the campaign · 527 groups = outside groups named for a tax law section · issue advocacy = pushing for a policy issue · transparency = being open to public view · accountability = being answerable for what you do

Part 6 of 12

Who Votes and Who Does Not

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 5: Identify the demographic factors — including education, age, and income — that most strongly predict voter turnout, and explain how structural barriers like registration requirements and election timing contribute to the "participatory gap" in American democracy.

IN MY WORDS: Do you know anyone who is old enough to vote but does not? What reasons do they give?

Reading VHow Many Americans Vote?

The structural mechanics of primary elections, the Electoral College, and campaign finance regulation all shape the competitive environment of American elections. But the ultimate variable — the factor that ultimately determines who holds power in a democratic republic — is who actually shows up to vote. The study of voter behavior and political participation is one of the most extensively researched areas of American political science, and its findings reveal both the remarkable persistence of certain patterns and the real consequences of the "participatory gap" — the systematic underrepresentation of certain segments of the electorate in the actual exercise of democratic power.

American voter turnout is, by the standards of comparable democracies, relatively low. In presidential elections — when turnout is at its highest — the United States has typically seen between 55 and 65 percent of the voting-eligible population cast a ballot, a figure that places it near the bottom of established democracies when measured against comparable contests. In midterm congressional elections, when the presidency is not on the ballot, turnout typically falls to between 35 and 45 percent. In state and local elections, which often determine policies of direct and immediate significance to citizens' daily lives — school board composition, local tax rates, zoning decisions — turnout can fall to the single digits in some jurisdictions. This pattern means that the decisions made in elections that formally represent the "consent of the governed" often reflect the preferences of a minority — and a demographically skewed minority — of the population.

Word help: participatory gap = the difference between who is eligible to vote and who actually does · voter turnout = the share of eligible people who vote · voting-eligible population = people who are allowed to vote · midterm = an election in the middle of a president's term · consent of the governed = the idea that government gets its power from the people · skewed = tilted toward one group

Chapter 14, Section IV, “The Demographics of Participation.”

Reading WEducation and Turnout

The single most powerful predictor of individual voter turnout is education level. Americans with college degrees vote at substantially higher rates than those without, and the gap widens further at the extremes: Americans with advanced degrees vote at very high rates, while those who have not completed high school vote at very low rates. This relationship between education and turnout holds across demographic groups, across types of elections, and across decades of survey research. The mechanism is not difficult to identify: higher education develops the information-processing skills that make navigating the voting process less cognitively demanding, increases awareness of political issues and their personal relevance, and reinforces social norms of civic participation that treat voting as an expected and important behavior. Education also typically increases income, and higher income correlates independently with higher turnout — wealthier Americans have more flexible work schedules, more easily available transportation, and greater confidence that their participation in the political process will produce tangible benefits.

Word help: predictor = something that helps you guess what will happen · advanced degrees = degrees beyond college · cognitively demanding = hard on the brain · reinforces = makes stronger · social norms = shared rules about how to act · correlates = goes together with · tangible = real and noticeable

Chapter 14, Section IV, “The Demographics of Participation.”

Reading XAge and Turnout

Age is the second most powerful predictor of voter turnout. Older Americans vote at dramatically higher rates than younger ones — a pattern so consistent that it has been a near-constant feature of American political participation data for decades. The turnout gap between the youngest eligible voters (18-to-24-year-olds) and the oldest cohorts (those over 65) typically exceeds thirty percentage points in presidential elections and is even larger in off-year and local contests. The consequences of this gap are significant: policies affecting younger Americans — student loan costs, entry-level job markets, long-term environmental policy — are decided by electorates that substantially over-represent the elderly, while the interests of younger citizens are correspondingly under-weighted.

Word help: cohorts = groups born around the same time · percentage points = the unit used to measure a gap between two percents · off-year = an election year with no presidential race · over-represent = to include more than their share · under-weighted = counted for less than they should be

Chapter 14, Section IV, “The Demographics of Participation.”

Reading the chart. In 2020, how big was the gap between the oldest and youngest group shown, and between the most and least educated group? Which gap was larger? Use Reading X and Reading W to say what the chapter says about the effects.

Reading YBeyond Individual Factors

The relatively low voter turnout rates of the United States compared to other established democracies cannot be fully explained by individual-level factors like education, age, and income. A significant portion of the turnout gap between the United States and comparable democracies is attributable to structural features of the American electoral system — specific rules and institutional arrangements that systematically increase the practical difficulty of voting for segments of the population that are already less inclined to participate.

Word help: individual-level factors = traits of each person, like age or income · attributable = caused by · structural features = rules and systems built into elections · institutional arrangements = how organizations and rules are set up · systematically = in a regular, built-in way

Chapter 14, Section IV, “Structural Barriers and the Architecture of Non-Participation.”

Reading ZRegistration

The most significant structural barrier is the voter registration requirement. The United States is one of the few established democracies in which citizens must take an affirmative action to register to vote before they can participate in elections — and in most states, this action must be completed weeks before the election itself, at a moment when many citizens are not yet paying attention to the upcoming contest. Countries like Canada, Australia, and most of Western Europe use automatic or "opt-out" voter registration systems, in which citizens are automatically enrolled on voter rolls upon reaching voting age or upon interacting with government agencies, and must take action to be removed rather than to be included. The practical effect of the American registration requirement is to impose an additional decision and action on potential voters before they can exercise the franchise — a requirement that falls most heavily on those who move frequently, have limited experience navigating bureaucratic processes, or simply do not think ahead to the deadline when they are not yet engaged with the election.

Word help: voter registration = signing up in advance to be allowed to vote · affirmative action = something you must do yourself · automatic or opt-out registration = being signed up unless you choose to leave · franchise = the right to vote · bureaucratic = about government paperwork and offices

Chapter 14, Section IV, “Structural Barriers and the Architecture of Non-Participation.”

Visual HWaiting to Register or Vote

This photograph appears in the chapter. It shows people waiting in a long line.

What to look for: Count how many people are waiting. Think about how a long wait could matter more to a worker with little free time.

Voters waiting in a long line to register or cast ballots. Image from the chapter (Chapter 14, Figure 6).

Reading AATuesday and Political Efficacy

The timing of American elections creates an additional structural barrier. Federal elections are held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November — a day that is not a federal holiday, that falls in the middle of a work and school week, and that requires most working Americans to arrange their lives around their voting participation. In contrast, many other democracies hold elections on weekends, make Election Day a national holiday, or provide multi-day voting periods that allow citizens to choose the time most convenient for them. The Tuesday election requirement falls most heavily on hourly workers, those with inflexible work schedules, and those who must arrange childcare or transportation — disproportionately working-class and lower-income Americans who are also, not coincidentally, less likely to vote for other reasons.

The concept of political efficacy — the individual's sense that their participation in the political process is meaningful and that the political system is genuinely responsive to their preferences — is closely connected to voter turnout and represents a psychological dimension of the participatory gap. Surveys consistently find that Americans who believe their vote matters and that the political system can be influenced by ordinary citizens turn out to vote at higher rates than those who feel that political outcomes are determined by forces beyond their control. Low political efficacy — the sense that the system is rigged, that one's vote is meaningless, or that all candidates are the same — is particularly common among lower-income Americans and members of communities that have historical reasons for skepticism about the responsiveness of political institutions to their interests.

Word help: hourly workers = people paid by the hour who often cannot leave work · inflexible = cannot be changed · political efficacy = the feeling that your participation matters and the system responds · responsiveness = how well something answers people's needs · skepticism = doubt · rigged = unfairly fixed

Chapter 14, Section IV, “Structural Barriers and the Architecture of Non-Participation.”

Part 7 of 12

Technology, Micro-Targeting, and the Chapter in Review

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 1: Essential Question: How do the structural mechanics of American elections shape the strategic behavior of candidates and the ultimate expression of popular sovereignty?

FQ 6: Assess the impact of modern technology and social media on political messaging, voter mobilization, and micro-targeting, and evaluate the democratic implications of campaigns' ability to deliver highly personalized political communications to distinct segments of the electorate.

IN MY WORDS: Have you ever seen an ad online that seemed to know a lot about you? How did it feel?

Reading ABMicro-Targeting

The transformation of political campaigning by digital technology has altered not only how campaigns communicate with voters but the granularity with which they can identify, analyze, and target specific segments of the electorate. The shift from the broadcast advertising model — in which campaigns spent the majority of their budgets on television advertisements that reached large, demographically mixed audiences with a common message — to the micro-targeting model of the digital era represents one of the most consequential changes in campaign strategy in the past quarter century.

Modern campaigns compile and analyze vast databases of voter information — combining official voter file data with commercial consumer data, social media activity, subscription records, and a wide range of other sources — to construct detailed profiles of individual voters that allow campaigns to predict with considerable accuracy which voters are likely to support their candidate, which are genuinely persuadable, which are unlikely to vote without targeted mobilization effort, and which specific issues, appeals, or messengers are most likely to resonate with each individual. This analytical capacity allows campaigns to radically increase the efficiency of their resource allocation: rather than delivering the same message to everyone, they can deliver customized messages to specific voters — pro-environmental appeals to voters identified as environmentally concerned, economic security messages to voters identified as economically anxious, public safety appeals to voters identified as concerned about crime — at a fraction of the cost of broadcasting a single message to everyone.

Word help: micro-targeting = sending different messages to small groups of voters · granularity = how fine and detailed something is · broadcast = sent out to a wide audience at once · voter file = the official list of voters · persuadable = able to be convinced · mobilization = getting supporters to act · customized = made for one person or group · efficiency = getting more done with less

Chapter 14, Section IV, “Technology, Micro-Targeting, and the Future of Political Mobilization.”

Two ways to reach voters | Use Reading AB. Write short phrases for each model.

Model — How does it work?
The broadcast model
What did a campaign send, and to whom?
The micro-targeting model
What does a campaign do now?
Reading ACA Contested Question

The democratic implications of micro-targeting are contested and complex. Proponents argue that personalized political communication is more effective at informing voters about issues that are genuinely relevant to their lives and more efficient at mobilizing citizens who might otherwise not participate. Critics argue that micro-targeting enables campaigns to say different — and sometimes contradictory — things to different audiences without the accountability that comes from public political communication, that it facilitates the manipulation of voters through emotional appeals tailored to their specific vulnerabilities, and that it contributes to the fragmentation of the political information environment in ways that make it harder for citizens to form shared understandings of public problems and their solutions.

Word help: proponents = people who support something · critics = people who oppose or question it · contradictory = saying the opposite of something else · accountability = being answerable for what you say · manipulation = tricking or steering someone · vulnerabilities = weak points · fragmentation = breaking into small pieces · shared understandings = things most people agree are true

Chapter 14, Section IV, “Technology, Micro-Targeting, and the Future of Political Mobilization.”

Reading ADFour Distortions

The primary system, designed to democratize nominations by taking the decision away from party bosses, has produced new forms of skew: the outsized influence of early states, the advantages of well-funded and well-known candidates, and the disproportionate power of intensely partisan primary voters over the choices available to the broader electorate. The Electoral College, designed to moderate the selection of the president through the judgment of deliberate electors, has become a system that concentrates presidential campaigns in a small number of swing states while leaving most of the country's voters on the political sidelines. The campaign finance system, designed to balance the constitutional protection of political speech with democratic concerns about corruption, has produced an environment in which unlimited outside spending has created new forms of influence that formal contribution limits cannot reach.

The patterns of voter participation that determine who actually exercises the formal right to vote compound these structural distortions. A political system in which higher-income, better-educated, and older Americans vote at dramatically higher rates than their lower-income, less-educated, and younger counterparts is a system in which the effective electorate is systematically different from the eligible electorate — and in which the policies produced by electoral competition are likely to reflect the preferences of those who participate more faithfully than those of the broader public.

Word help: democratize = make more open to ordinary people · skew = a tilt toward one side · swing states = states that could go either way · sidelines = out of the action · effective electorate = the people who really vote · eligible electorate = everyone allowed to vote · compound = make worse together

Chapter 14, Conclusion.

Putting it together. Use Reading AD and Reading AB. Pick two features of elections from this chapter (such as primaries, the Electoral College, campaign money, turnout, or micro-targeting) and explain how together they affect whose preferences are heard most.

Reading AENot Immutable

None of these structural features is immutable. Voter registration rules can be reformed; the Electoral College can be modified by interstate compact or constitutional amendment; campaign finance law can be restructured within the boundaries the First Amendment permits; primary calendar rules can be changed by party action without any legislative requirement. Whether any of these reforms will occur, and in what form, will depend on the same political competition this chapter has examined — the contest among organized interests, parties, and citizens over the rules that govern the exercise of democratic power.

Word help: immutable = unchangeable · interstate compact = an agreement among states · constitutional amendment = a change to the Constitution · legislative requirement = a law passed by a legislature · party action = decisions made by the party itself · competition = a contest

Chapter 14, Conclusion.

Part 8 of 12

Press Freedom, the Gatekeeper, and the Watchdog

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 7: Essential Question: How does the media serve as a "gatekeeper" and "watchdog" to influence the strategic priorities of the American government?

FQ 8: Analyze the media's three primary functions — gatekeeper, watchdog, and scorekeeper — and explain how each shapes the flow of political information between citizens and government in a representative democracy.

FQ 9: Evaluate the impact of agenda setting and framing on public opinion and the legislative process, explaining how the choice of which stories to cover and how to present them constitutes a consequential form of political power.

IN MY WORDS: Think of one news story you saw this week. Who decided it was worth your attention?

Reading AFThe Pentagon Papers

On June 13, 1971, the New York Times began publishing excerpts from a classified Defense Department study that would come to be known as the Pentagon Papers — a seven-thousand-page internal history of American decision-making in Vietnam that revealed, in meticulous detail, that four successive administrations had systematically misled the public and Congress about the nature, scope, and prospects of the war. The Nixon administration immediately sought a court order blocking further publication, arguing that the release of classified information endangered national security. Seventeen days later, the Supreme Court ruled against the government in a landmark First Amendment decision that has shaped the legal relationship between the press and government ever since. The Court held, in New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), that the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify prior restraint of publication — that even in matters of national security, the press retained the right to publish information it had obtained, and the government's remedy lay in prosecuting those who leaked classified information, not in silencing the newspapers that printed it.

Word help: Pentagon Papers = a secret Defense Department history of the Vietnam War · classified = kept secret by the government · prior restraint = stopping something from being published before it appears · landmark = a very important decision · First Amendment = the part of the Constitution that protects free speech and a free press · leaked = given out in secret · misled = gave false ideas to

Chapter 15, Introduction.

Source CJustice Black on a Free Press

Justice Hugo Black wrote this in a separate opinion that agreed with the Court's decision in the Pentagon Papers case, New York Times Co. v. United States (1971).

“In the First Amendment the Founding Fathers gave the free press the protection it must have to fulfill its essential role in our democracy. The press was to serve the governed, not the governors. The Government's power to censor the press was abolished so that the press would remain forever free to censure the Government. The press was protected so that it could bare the secrets of government and inform the people.”

Word help: essential = necessary · role = job · the governed = the people who are ruled · the governors = the people who rule · censor = to block or cut out speech or writing · censure = to criticize strongly · bare = to uncover and show

Justice Hugo Black, concurring opinion, New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U.S. 713 (1971). Cornell Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/403/713). Primary source.

Whom does the press serve? Use Black's words and Reading AF. Explain what Black means by “serve the governed, not the governors,” and how the Pentagon Papers case fits.

Reading AGThree Roles at Once

The American media does not occupy a single, unified role in the political system. Rather, it performs multiple distinct functions simultaneously — sometimes in tension with each other — each of which shapes the relationship between citizens and government in different ways. Political scientists have identified three functions as most fundamental to the media's democratic significance: the gatekeeper function, through which the media determines which events and issues receive public attention; the watchdog function, through which the media investigates and exposes government misconduct; and the scorekeeper function, through which the media tracks and interprets the competitive dynamics of political contest. Understanding each function, and the tensions among them, is essential to understanding the media's role in the American political system.

Word help: unified = all one thing · gatekeeper function = deciding which stories get attention · watchdog function = investigating government misconduct · scorekeeper function = tracking who is winning a political contest · competitive dynamics = how a contest is going · in tension = pulling against each other

Chapter 15, Section I, “The Media's Three Roles.”

Reading AHThe Gatekeeper and Agenda Setting

The gatekeeper function is perhaps the most powerful of the media's political roles, precisely because it is the least visible. When a journalist decides that a particular story is worth covering — and by implication, that thousands of other potential stories are not — they are making a consequential political decision, even if it is framed as a purely professional judgment about newsworthiness. The stories that appear in the news shape what citizens think about, what concerns they bring to their representatives, what issues politicians believe they must address, and ultimately what problems the government attempts to solve. Stories that do not appear might as well not exist from the standpoint of democratic politics, because the public and its representatives have no reliable way to know about issues that the media has not reported.

The concept of agenda setting, developed most systematically by political scientists Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw in their landmark study of the 1968 presidential election, captures this gatekeeping power in its political dimension. McCombs and Shaw found a striking correspondence between the issues that local newspapers covered most prominently in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, and the issues that voters in that community identified as the most important problems facing the country. The media did not tell voters what to think about these issues — but it powerfully influenced which issues they thought about at all. The causal mechanism is straightforward: most citizens have no direct experience with most policy questions and depend entirely on media coverage to know that those issues exist, what arguments are being made about them, and how urgently they deserve attention. A media that devotes sustained, prominent coverage to the federal deficit signals to its audience that the deficit is an important problem; a media that ignores the deficit signals that it is not, regardless of whether the deficit is actually growing or shrinking.

Word help: gatekeeper = someone who decides what passes through · newsworthiness = how important a story seems · agenda setting = the media's power to make some issues seem important · McCombs and Shaw = two researchers who studied the 1968 election · correspondence = a close match · federal deficit = the amount the government spends beyond what it takes in

Reading AIAgenda Setting Reaches Government

The practical consequences of agenda setting extend well beyond individual public opinion and into the operation of the legislative process. Congressional committees schedule hearings, introduce legislation, and conduct oversight investigations in response to issues that have achieved sufficient public visibility — and public visibility is substantially a function of media coverage. Regulatory agencies develop and enforce rules in areas that attract media attention, while neglecting issues that do not. Presidents develop and announce policy initiatives in response to the pressure of a media-driven public agenda. The agenda-setting power of the media means that the decision about which stories to cover — made daily by editors, producers, and reporters across thousands of media organizations — is, in aggregate, a consequential exercise of political power, even when it is made on entirely commercial or professional grounds.

Word help: legislative process = how laws are made · oversight investigations = Congress checking on how the government is working · visibility = how easily something is seen · regulatory agencies = government offices that write and enforce rules · initiatives = new plans · in aggregate = all together

Reading AJThe Watchdog

The watchdog function of the press represents its most constitutionally significant role — the function that most directly animates the First Amendment's protection of press freedom and most clearly articulates the relationship between independent journalism and democratic self-governance. The theory underlying watchdog journalism is straightforward: those who hold power will, in the absence of external accountability, tend to abuse it. The mechanisms of democratic accountability built into the Constitution — elections, separation of powers, legislative oversight — are powerful but imperfect. They operate on irregular cycles, they depend on information that powerful actors can often suppress, and they are subject to the same political pressures they are supposed to check. An independent press that investigates government conduct continuously, that is legally protected from government interference, and that has both the institutional interest and the professional capacity to uncover what those in power would prefer to conceal provides a form of accountability that complements and reinforces the constitutional structure.

Word help: watchdog = someone who guards against wrongdoing · animates = gives life to · accountability = being answerable for your actions · separation of powers = dividing power among branches · oversight = checking on work · suppress = to hide or stop · complements = adds to

Chapter 15, Section I, “The Watchdog.”

Visual JA Hearing Room During Watergate

This photograph appears in the chapter. It shows a hearing room with press and officials in the Watergate era.

What to look for: Look at the microphones and the audience. Congress and the press both investigated what happened. Think about what each one adds.

Reading AKWatchdogs in History

The history of American investigative journalism is, in significant part, the history of democratic accountability operating through nongovernmental channels. The muckraking journalists of the Progressive era — Ida Tarbell's investigation of Standard Oil's monopolistic practices, Upton Sinclair's exposure of conditions in the meatpacking industry, Lincoln Steffens's documentation of municipal corruption across major American cities — produced public outrage that translated directly into legislative action, including the Sherman Antitrust Act's enforcement, the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, and a wave of municipal reform. The exposure of the Watergate scandal by Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, beginning in 1972, uncovered a pattern of criminal conduct in the Nixon White House that eventually produced the first presidential resignation in American history. The publication of the Pentagon Papers forced a public reckoning with the gap between the official narrative of American success in Vietnam and the internal government assessment that the war was being lost.

Each of these episodes illustrates the watchdog function at its most consequential — journalism producing accountability that the ordinary political process had failed to generate. They also illustrate why the watchdog function depends on institutional conditions that are not automatically maintained: the financial capacity to support time-intensive investigative reporting, the editorial independence to pursue stories that powerful interests would prefer be suppressed, the legal protection against government retaliation for publication of embarrassing or classified information, and the professional norms that distinguish investigative journalism from mere rumor-mongering or partisan attack. When these conditions erode — as critics argue they have in significant respects in the contemporary media environment — the watchdog function weakens, and the accountability it provides is diminished.

Word help: investigative journalism = long, deep reporting to uncover hidden wrongdoing · muckraking = Progressive-era reporting that exposed corruption · Standard Oil = a huge oil company criticized for monopoly · Pure Food and Drug Act = the 1906 law on food and medicine safety · municipal = about a city · editorial independence = freedom to choose what to report · rumor-mongering = spreading unproven stories

Part 9 of 12

The Scorekeeper, Framing, and the Marketplace of Ideas

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 8: Analyze the media's three primary functions — gatekeeper, watchdog, and scorekeeper — and explain how each shapes the flow of political information between citizens and government in a representative democracy.

FQ 9: Evaluate the impact of agenda setting and framing on public opinion and the legislative process, explaining how the choice of which stories to cover and how to present them constitutes a consequential form of political power.

FQ 10: Explain how the transition from the broadcasting era of three dominant television networks to the narrowcasting era of cable news and digital media has contributed to selective exposure, echo chambers, and political polarization.

IN MY WORDS: When you hear a poll say a candidate is ahead, does it change how you feel about the race? Why?

Reading ALHorse-Race Journalism

The third major function the media performs — the scorekeeper role during election campaigns — represents a significant departure from the civic ideals that animate the watchdog and gatekeeper functions. Horse-race journalism, as it is disparagingly known, refers to the pattern in which media coverage of electoral campaigns focuses disproportionately on the competitive dynamics of the race — who is ahead in the polls, which candidate had a good week and which had a bad one, what the latest fundraising numbers reveal about relative momentum — at the expense of substantive engagement with the policy questions that the election is nominally about.

The incentives that produce horse-race journalism are not difficult to identify, and they are deeply embedded in the commercial logic of the modern media industry. Electoral competition, like athletic competition, has a natural drama that makes it engaging to audiences regardless of their level of policy interest: there are winners and losers, momentum shifts, unexpected developments, and a definitive resolution that satisfies the narrative structure of a story. Polling data provides a continuous stream of quantifiable updates that can be reported, graphed, and analyzed on a daily basis, creating the appearance of informative content with minimal investment in the substantive expertise required to evaluate competing policy proposals. The horse-race frame also has the advantage of apparent neutrality — reporting on who is winning avoids the editorial judgment required to evaluate whose policy positions are more sound, more fiscally responsible, or more consistent with the candidate's own record.

Word help: scorekeeper = the media role of tracking who is winning · horse-race journalism = news that focuses on who is ahead instead of policy · momentum = a sense that a candidate is gaining · substantive = about real content · incentives = reasons that push people to act · commercial logic = the need to earn money · apparent neutrality = looking fair without taking a side

Chapter 15, Section I, “The Scorekeeper: Elections as Horse Race.”

Reading AMWhat Horse-Race Coverage Costs

The consequences of horse-race journalism for democratic deliberation are significant and well-documented. Studies of election news coverage consistently find that the proportion of coverage devoted to polls, strategy, and competitive dynamics dramatically exceeds the proportion devoted to policy substance in most media outlets. Candidates whose campaign narratives are shaped by the scorekeeper media learn to perform for the daily news cycle rather than to engage substantively with complex policy questions — to generate the kind of dramatic moments, pointed attacks, and memorable sound bites that drive competitive coverage rather than the kind of detailed, nuanced policy discussion that would enable citizens to make genuinely informed electoral choices. The result is an information environment in which many voters know who is winning but are poorly equipped to evaluate which candidate's proposals for healthcare, immigration, or economic policy would actually serve their interests.

Word help: deliberation = careful public discussion · well-documented = shown clearly by research · competitive dynamics = how the contest is going · news cycle = the daily rush of news · sound bites = short, catchy quotes · nuanced = careful about details · informed electoral choices = voting choices based on knowing the facts

Reading ANWhat Is Framing?

If the gatekeeper function determines which events and issues receive public attention, the framing function determines how the events and issues that do receive coverage are understood. Framing is the process through which media organizations — through their choice of language, images, experts, and narrative context — provide an interpretive lens through which audiences make sense of political events. The same set of facts, presented within different frames, can produce dramatically different public reactions and political consequences. Understanding how framing works, why it is so powerful, and how both media organizations and political actors use it strategically is essential to becoming an informed consumer of political information.

A frame, in the political communication sense, is a way of organizing and presenting information that emphasizes certain aspects of reality while de-emphasizing others — that makes some considerations more cognitively accessible when audiences evaluate an issue, while pushing others into the background. Frames are not necessarily fabrications or distortions; a reporter who covers a labor strike by focusing on the economic demands of the workers and a reporter who covers the same strike by focusing on the disruption to commerce and the public inconvenience are both reporting accurately on real aspects of the situation. But the frame each chooses will shape how their audience understands the event — who is sympathetic and who is not, what is at stake, and what kind of response is appropriate.

Word help: framing = the way a story is described, which shapes how people understand it · interpretive lens = a way of looking that gives meaning · cognitively accessible = easy to think of · fabrications = made-up things · distortions = twisted versions · labor strike = workers stopping work to demand changes · commerce = business

Visual LThe Big Type War of the Yellow Kids

What to look for: The two men are rival newspaper owners. Notice that both are shouting about war. Think about how loud headlines can shape what people feel.
